bio.en: Gergely Orosz is the author of The Pragmatic Engineer, the top engineering newsletter on Substack, which he writes full-time after leaving a senior engineering role at Uber.
bio.zh: Gergely Orosz 是《The Pragmatic Engineer》的作者，这是 Substack 上排名第一的工程师 newsletter，他在离开 Uber 的高级工程职位后全职写作。

summary.en: Gergely shares what it's actually like to go full-time as a newsletter creator—the day-to-day life, the pros and cons, and why leaving a lucrative Uber job (where he made ~$330K) turned out to pay even better with no theoretical cap. He and Lenny compare notes as two full-time newsletter writers, covering what it takes to succeed and how to get started if you're curious about the creator route. It's a candid, behind-the-scenes look at building a career as an independent writer.
summary.zh: Gergely 分享了全职做 newsletter 创作者的真实体验——日常工作、利弊，以及为何离开 Uber 那份高薪工作（年薪约 33 万美元）后，收入反而没有了理论上限、变得更高。他和 Lenny 作为两位全职 newsletter 写作者交流心得，聊了成功需要什么，以及如果你想走创作者路线该如何起步。这是一期关于独立写作者职业生涯的坦诚幕后分享。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: In my best year at Uber, I made about 320 or $330,000 in total compensation. And when I quit my job, I was actually thinking, am I crazy? Because I am leaving... Especially in Europe, this is a lot of money [inaudible 00:00:14] this will be similar to something... Someone in a similar position would've made five or 600K in total in the U.S. But now I am making more in compensation that I made at Uber. And the difference is that now my compensation... Well, my earnings keep going up as long as the newsletter is growing, so there's no theoretical cap on this. Of course there's an actual cap, there's churn, growth is slowing over time. But it's very, very strange, because I felt that I was in a really privileged position, just honestly making tons of money, doing a job that I loved. And this was at Uber or as a software engineer. And I'm now doing stuff that I love, and in some strange way, I guess it even pays better.
turns.zh: 在优步（Uber）效力的最佳年份，我的总薪酬约为32万美元。离职时，我甚至在想——我是不是疯了？毕竟我要离开了……尤其是在欧洲，这笔钱可真不少[00:00:14无法听清]。这笔收入在美国类似职位的人可能达到50万到60万美元。但现在我的收入比在优步时还要高。而且关键是，只要我的通讯订阅量持续增长，我的收入就会不断攀升——理论上没有上限。当然实际会有天花板，用户流失率会逐渐上升。但这感觉太奇怪了，因为我曾觉得自己处在一个非常优越的位置，轻松赚大钱，还做着自己热爱的工作——无论是在优步还是作为软件工程师。如今我依然从事着自己热爱的事业，奇妙的是收入甚至更高了。

In this episode, we talk about the life of newslettering full time, like we both do. turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Gergely, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 格尔格利，欢迎来到我们的播客。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: It's awesome. Great to be here, Lenny.
turns.zh: 太棒了。很高兴来到这里，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think this is going to be a pretty special and unique podcast. Your newsletter is the number one technology newsletter on Substack, called the Pragmatic Engineer, by the way. My newsletter is the number one business newsletter on Substack, and so we're connected in this really special, weird way, and I thought it would be pretty fun to just explore this weird path that we're on doing this newsletter thing, and in that, help listeners understand the pros and cons of this life, how to go down this route, what it takes to be successful, all that stuff. But before we get into all that, I'd love for you to spend maybe a minute just giving us a little overview of your career, and how you got to where you are today doing this newsletter, and what you spend your time on now.
turns.zh: 我觉得这将是一场非常特别且独特的播客。顺便说一句，你的Substack新闻通讯《务实工程师》是Substack上排名第一的科技新闻通讯。而我的Substack新闻通讯是Substack上排名第一的商业新闻通讯。因此，我们以一种非常特别、奇特的方式产生了联系。我觉得探讨我们做新闻通讯这件事的奇特之路会非常有趣，同时还能帮助听众理解这种生活方式的利弊、如何走上这条道路、需要具备哪些成功要素等等。但在深入探讨这些之前，我希望你能花一分钟时间简要介绍一下你的职业生涯，以及你如何走到今天经营新闻通讯的位置，以及你现在的工作内容。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: My career started out as what you might consider a pretty typical software engineer career. I graduated from university, I did a computer science degree for a five year program, so I did bachelor's and master's. I worked on the side, I hacked around, built small websites here and there, and during university I worked at a small web agency. And then I worked my way up in the industry. So I started off at a consulting company, we were just building for other companies. I'm originally from Hungary, in Europe. I then moved to UK, which was a big step up for me in terms of just getting access to, I guess, more modern software development. I was at a consulting company there as well. And I moved up to London, which in Europe, I feel it's like the New York of Europe, or even the Silicon Valley, back in the day. Back before Brexit, it was the biggest tech hub.
turns.zh: 我的职业生涯始于你可能认为非常典型的软件工程师之路。我大学毕业，完成了为期五年的计算机科学学士和硕士学位。在校期间，我在一家小型网络代理公司兼职，开发一些小型网站。毕业后，我在一家咨询公司工作，主要为其他公司开发软件。我来自欧洲的匈牙利，之后搬到了英国。这对我来说是一个巨大的进步，因为我得以接触到更现代的软件开发技术。我在英国的咨询公司也获得了晋升。后来我搬到了伦敦，在欧洲人眼中，伦敦就像是纽约，甚至是硅谷的缩影。在英国脱欧之前，它是最大的科技中心。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I worked at an investment bank there, and then on the side I was always building mobile apps, and I got into Skype. I like to say Skype, but it was Microsoft. They just bought Skype at that point, and it was a lot more startup-y environment, a lot more fast moving. I then moved to another startup where I was a founding engineer of a acquisition. It's a startup called Skyscanner. And then I ended up at Uber at Amsterdam, where I joined as a senior software engineer, and I became a manager, and then a manager of managers, and it was just... I feel, looking back at that part of my career, I just felt really growing all the time, just taking each step one step at a time, which gave me a lot of appreciation for all these levels.
turns.zh: 我曾在当地一家投资银行工作，业余时间一直开发移动应用，后来接触到Skype。我喜欢说Skype，但那时候它还是微软旗下公司。当时微软刚收购Skype，那里的创业氛围更浓厚，发展速度也更快。之后我加入了另一家初创公司Skyscanner，担任创始工程师，参与收购项目。再后来，我转到了阿姆斯特丹的优步，担任高级软件工程师，后来晋升为经理，最终成为经理的管理者。在回顾这段职业生涯时，我觉得自己一直在不断成长，一步一个脚印，这让我对各个职级都心怀感激。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And then, just as I was on this really good career path, I was on the path to being a senior engineering manager, or who knows, one day I might have had a shot of being their director of engineering as well, I decided to leave Uber. And we'll talk about it a little later in the podcast, but I didn't plan like this, but I started writing a newsletter. And now here I am writing a newsletter where a bunch of people are reading it, and it's a really unexpected turn and a really cool life as well.
turns.zh: 就在我的职业生涯顺风顺水、即将晋升为高级工程经理，甚至有机会担任工程总监时，我却决定离开优步。我们稍后在播客中再详细聊这个决定，但当时我并没有刻意规划，只是开始写一份时事通讯。如今我写的这份时事通讯吸引了大量读者，这真是个意外之喜，也让我收获了全新的生活体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. On the newsletter, just to give people a little bit of context of how big this has gotten, can you share just a couple stats about the growth of the newsletter, the size, and anything else you want to share there?
turns.zh: 太棒了。关于这份时事通讯的规模，能否跟听众分享一下增长数据？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Just today I checked and it said 189,000 subscribers. I think the past 90 days has been growing with 80,000 subscribers, so it's almost a thousand people per day, which is incredible. Because these numbers are huge. If you're listening, you're probably thinking, "Wow." And that's how I feel every day as well. But I've been writing a blog for many, many years, and these are numbers I never thought it would be. And the growth just seems to be accelerating. There was a tipping point in April where the newsletter was growing... In the first about nine months of the newsletter, it got to 50,000 subscribers, and then the next five months, or six or seven months, it went up by another a hundred and something thousand subscribers. This was when Substack introduced recommendations, which has been a massive growth engine, and I guess being one of the top publications, I benefited from it. But those numbers are again...
turns.zh: 今天我查看，订阅用户达18.9万。过去90天新增8万订阅用户，平均每天近千人订阅，真是令人惊叹。这些数字太庞大了。听众可能觉得不可思议，我每天也感慨不已。但我写博客多年，从未想过能达到这样的规模。增长速度还在加速。4月份有个转折点，时事通讯迎来爆发式增长……前九个月订阅用户增长5万，之后五六个月又新增了十几万。这得益于Substack推出的推荐机制，时事通讯成了主要增长引擎，作为头部账号，我也从中获益。但这些数字依然……

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So this is a paid newsletter as well. So there's a free version and a paid version, and there's thousands of people paying for the newsletter. It's a single digit percentage, but it's a very, very healthy one. And again, it just beat all my expectations. And I guess we're in similar boats, because our newsletter setup, yours and mine, is somewhat similar. We have plenty of differences as well, but I make most of my revenue from subscriptions, and I don't do sponsorships or ads in the newsletter. So if people sign up for the free one, they get articles every now and then, and for the paid one, they get it a lot more and in more depth.
turns.zh: 这是一份付费时事通讯，有免费版和付费版，数千人为其付费。虽然付费率仅个位数，但收入非常可观。我们的时事通讯模式和你的有些相似，也有许多不同之处。我主要靠订阅收入，不在通讯中投放广告或赞助内容。免费版用户偶尔能收到文章，付费版则有更多深度内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you give listeners a sense of just the order of magnitude income you make from this, versus your cushy tech job at Uber? You don't have to share numbers or anything like that.
turns.zh: 能否让听众了解一下你从这份时事通讯获得的收入规模，与你在优步的优渥职位相比如何？无需具体数字。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Yeah. I'll share a little numbers of my cushy tech job at Uber. I was in Europe, and European tech salaries, or I'll say total compensation, will be lower than for example the U.S., but it'll be higher than let's say regions like India or Indonesia. There's regional differences, and this is true for big tech as well. Uber was a good example on this. But in my best year at Uber, I made about 320 or $330,000 in total compensation. This was after Uber went public, so it includes the stock, the base salary, the bonus, which was very, very good in Europe. And when I quit my job, I was actually thinking, "Am I crazy? Because I'm leaving..." Especially in Europe, this is a lot of money [inaudible 00:09:53] this will be similar to something... Someone in a similar position would've made five or 600 K in total in the U.S.
turns.zh: 是的。我来分享一下我在优步（Uber）这份轻松科技工作的收入数据。我在欧洲工作，那里的科技行业薪资，或者说整体薪酬水平，确实比美国低，但比印度或印度尼西亚等地区要高。这里存在地区差异，科技巨头也是如此。优步就是一个很好的例子。但我在优步最辉煌的年份，综合薪酬达到了32万美元。这是在优步上市后计算的，包括股票、基本工资和奖金，在欧洲这已经非常丰厚了。当我离职时，心里其实在想：“我疯了吗？毕竟要离开……”尤其是在欧洲，这笔钱确实很高[00:09:53语音不清]，但在美国类似职位的人综合收入可能达到50万到60万美元。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So I walked away from that, and I was pretty sure that I'll just [inaudible 00:10:04] a lot less, but I'll enjoy what I'm doing, or I'll have... I'll just give it a go. But now I am making more in compensation that I made at Uber. And the difference is that now my compensation, my earnings, keep going up as long as the newsletter is growing, so there's no theoretical cap on this. Of course there is an actual cap, there's churn, growth is slowing over time, but it's very, very strange, because I felt that I was in a really privileged position, just honestly making tons of money, doing a job that I loved. And this was at Uber or as a software engineer. And I'm now doing stuff that I love, and in some strange way, I guess it even pays better. Part of it is just luck, part of this is situational. I think we're going to talk a bit more about this. But this was very, very surprising and very unexpected for me.
turns.zh: 所以我离开了那份工作，心里很清楚自己可能会赚得少很多，但只要我热爱这份工作，就会继续坚持。但现在我的收入比在优步时还要高。这其中的关键在于，只要订阅用户数量持续增长，我的收入就会不断攀升，所以理论上没有上限。当然实际会有天花板，用户流失率也会随时间放缓，但这种情况很奇特，因为我曾觉得自己身处一个非常优越的位置，赚着大把的钱，做着自己热爱的工作——无论是在优步还是作为软件工程师。而现在我做着自己热爱的事情，奇妙的是收入甚至更高了。这既有运气成分，也有机遇因素。我想我们今天会深入探讨这个话题，但这对我来说确实是个令人惊讶且出乎意料的转变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's a great segue to the first thing I want to talk about, but just to frame what I want to spend our time on today, there's these four areas I want to explore. One is your decision to leave and start this life of writing, which is a very non-traditional life. Two is what the life of a paid newsletter person is like. What do you do all day? How do you find time to do this? How do you produce so much content? Three, what it takes to be successful at this. A lot of people... I always say it's easy to start a newsletter, hard to keep it going, and I'm curious what you find is important to be successful. And then four, how do you get started if you want to start your own newsletter?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这为我接下来想谈的第一点做了很好的铺垫，但先简要说明一下我们今天要探讨的四个主题。第一个是关于你决定离开优步，开始这份写作生涯的决定——这是一条非传统的职业道路。第二个是付费订阅通讯从业者的日常生活：你每天都在做什么？如何挤出时间？如何产出如此海量的内容？第三个是成功的关键因素——很多人……我常说创办通讯容易，但持续运营难，我很想了解你认为成功的关键因素。第四个是如果你想创办自己的通讯，该如何起步？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But before I get into that, I just wanted to add a thought that I had. The way I think about this life in terms of comparing to the old job is, one, it feels instead of one boss, I have thousands of micro bosses, and one of them can fire me and many do every day, but it feels safer than at a tech job where one person can decide. And then the other piece is, assuming it keeps growing, you're getting a raise almost every day, every week, depending on the growth rate, and that's cool.
turns.zh: 但在深入探讨这些话题之前，我想先补充一下我的感悟。把这份工作与我之前的科技工作相比，我觉得一方面是从单一老板转变为数千个“微老板”，其中任何一个都能随时解雇你（很多人每天都在这么做），但这比在科技公司由一人决定命运要安全得多。另一方面，假设订阅用户持续增长，你几乎每天、每周都能获得加薪，这真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: That is really cool. I had a spreadsheet that I maintained for the first year of the publication, where I listed, for every article, how much did my annual revenue go up a week later. So tracking what was the impact. And the crazy thing was that, when I wrote a really good article that resonated with people, sometimes it was an article that I thought was mediocre and people still loved it [inaudible 00:12:20] it was a really good article that I put tons of work in, I saw myself getting a raise. And this is just something you just don't get in corporate. I mean, it's by design, and there's a lot of good stuff about it, but I feel that this life, and we'll touch more on this, but there's a lot of surprising things, both good and bad, but this is a really good one. So for doing something awesome, you can just give yourself a raise, especially because this is just like you, mine is also a one person business right now.
turns.zh: 太酷了。我曾做过一份表格，记录了创业第一年的每篇文章一周后为我带来的年收入增长情况，这样就能追踪其影响力。最奇妙的是，当我写了一篇引发共鸣的好文章时，有时那篇我自认为平庸的文章却深受读者喜爱。而那些我投入大量心血的优质文章，反而让我获得了加薪机会。这在公司里是无法实现的。我承认，公司制度有其优点，但我觉得这种生活方式——稍后我们会深入探讨——有太多令人惊喜的元素，无论好坏，但这份工作带来的快乐确实无与伦比。尤其是当你能通过自己的努力给自己加薪时，尤其是在目前仍是一人公司的创业阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. So you're at Uber, you're making hundreds of thousands of dollars writing code, it's pretty sweet. Uber's growing. You probably got all these RSUs that are going to keep accumulating. It's pretty good. And you decide, "I'm going to try to make money on the internet writing," which is an obvious way to make a lot of money. Not. And so I'm curious, what got you to leave that job and explore writing and get to this writing path?
turns.zh: 是啊，好的。你在优步工作，写代码就能赚几十万美元，真是太棒了。优步在快速发展，你可能还获得了大量即将不断增值的限制性股票单位。这确实不错。但你却决定辞去优步的工作，转而尝试写作谋生，这条路显然更难走。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: The short of it is, it was a promise to myself, and COVID, and Uber doing layoffs. And the longer version is that, when I joined Uber, before Uber I was... Now we're talking numbers on my old job, but I was working in London as a principal engineer at Skyscanner. Skyscanner was a unicorn, one of the few unicorns in the UK, UK headquartered and all that, and I was making like 90-something thousand pounds in base salary, which is maybe a 120, 130, or $140,000, depends on how the pound is doing, or sometimes these days it's almost just the same. But back then that was a really good... And this was most of it. I got some stock as well. And I thought I was close to the top of the market in London. I knew people, and it seemed this was a really good compensation package.
turns.zh: 简而言之，这是我对自己的一个承诺，再加上新冠疫情，还有优步裁员的压力。更详细地说，我加入优步之前，在伦敦的Skyscanner担任首席工程师。Skyscanner曾是独角兽企业，英国为数不多的独角兽公司之一，总部设在英国，我当时的基本薪资约9万英镑，换算成美元约12万至13万，或者14万美元——这取决于英镑汇率，但如今汇率基本持平。不过那时这确实是高薪了。我的收入主要来自股票，并且我觉得自己在伦敦的薪资水平已经接近顶峰。我认识很多人，当时这份薪酬待遇看起来相当不错。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And then Uber called me up saying, "Do you want to interview?" I interviewed with them, they gave me an offer, and I negotiated, and they basically doubled my compensation. I was like, wow, this is [inaudible 00:14:16] I knew about Silicon Valley compensation, but I assumed that [inaudible 00:14:20] you're not going to get this, but Uber was getting something closer to that. So I told myself, all right, so I'm getting a really good deal, and most of it is stock, which is... Uber [inaudible 00:14:32] 2016, no-one knew if Uber will go public, although I suspected, because they contacted me to build a payments team so do a SOX compliant payment system. And you need a SOX compliant payment system if you want to go IPO.
turns.zh: 然后优步联系我说：“你想来面试吗？”我去面试了，他们给了我一份录用通知，我经过谈判后，他们把我的薪酬翻了一倍。我当时很惊讶，哇，[不清00:14:16] 我听说过硅谷的高薪，但以为自己拿不到这么高。但优步给的薪酬接近那个水平。所以我告诉自己，嗯，我得到了一个很好的交易，而且大部分是股票，这很棒……优步在2016年[不清00:14:32]，当时没人确定它是否会上市，不过我有所预感，因为他们联系我组建支付团队，开发符合SOX标准的支付系统。而要上市就必须有符合SOX标准的支付系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's funny. It reminds me at Airbnb, there's all these people trying to figure out, when are we going to go public? And then there's the team working on SOX stuff and Sarbanes-Oxley, this is good.
turns.zh: 真有意思。这让我想起在Airbnb时，所有人都急切想知道何时上市。而团队却在忙着SOX相关事务和萨班斯-奥克斯利法案的合规工作，这真是好事。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Yeah. So anyway, I said, all right, this is a massive lottery ticket. If it goes in, every year I make two years of salary, pretty much. That's how I was thinking. But if not, again, don't forget I'm in Europe where we're used to not seeing any returns on stock. So European software engineers will not value stock as much, because they just haven't seen success stories. So I told myself, if four years later Uber exits and I make a bunch of money, I owe it to myself to take a risk, because then I'll have four years of savings in my bank, which... Back then I had maybe six months of savings or something. So this was the promise to myself.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以不管怎样，我当时想，嗯，这是一张巨额彩票。如果中奖了，那我每年就能赚到两年的薪水差不多。这就是我的想法。但如果没中奖，别忘了，我在欧洲这边，习惯了股票投资没有回报。所以欧洲的软件工程师不太看重股票，因为他们根本没见过成功案例。所以我告诉自己，如果四年后优步退市，我赚了一大笔钱，那我就有义务去冒险，因为到时候我银行里有四年的积蓄……当时我可能只有六个月的储蓄之类的。所以这就是我对自己的承诺。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And then I probably would've forgotten about this, but four years later, almost on the dot, COVID starts, and it really hit super hard. We're laying off people, we had to lay off 20% of the engineers. I was already managing a group of about 30 people, I had managers under me, and 20% of the people or 15% had to be let go. And I was thinking to myself, what am I doing here? I looked ahead, Uber was going to have a really bad year, I'm going to have to manage morale. Up to then, I'd helped put together this team, and we had a really good charter, and we had to throw that charter out the window, because it made no sense with the economic reality. So I thought back, and I told myself, if I'll be here, I'll take a risk, and I'll try to do something else. So I was like, all right, let me pull this trigger.
turns.zh: 然后我可能已经把这事忘了，但四年后，几乎在同一时间点，新冠疫情来袭，冲击非常严重。我们开始裁员，裁掉了20%的工程师。我当时已经管理着一个约30人的团队，手下还有经理，而20%的人，也就是15%的人不得不被裁掉。我当时就在想，我在这儿干什么？我预见到优步那年会很糟糕，我得管理好团队士气。到那时，我已经帮着组建了这个团队，我们有过一个很好的规划书，但由于经济现实的原因，那个规划书根本没用了。所以我回想起来，告诉自己，如果我还要留在这儿，那就冒险一试，尝试做点别的。所以我说，好吧，让我按下这个扳机。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And my plan was very simple. Leave Uber and start a startup, raise venture capital, because I haven't done that before but it kind of runs in the family. My brother's on his second startup, and he sold his first one to Skyscanner, and now he's building this startup called Craft Docs. It's a really slick document editing system, they just raised their series B. So through him I know [inaudible 00:16:42] startup life is, and I felt I never did that, I always worked at big companies.
turns.zh: 我的计划很简单。离开优步，创办一家初创公司，筹集风险投资，因为我之前没做过这事，但这在我们家族里算常事。我兄弟正在经营他的第二家初创公司，他把第一家卖给了Skyscanner，现在他在做一个叫Craft Docs的初创项目。这是一个非常棒的文档编辑系统，他们刚完成B轮融资。所以通过他，我了解了初创公司的运作，我觉得自己从未涉足过这块领域，一直在大公司工作。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So my plan was [inaudible 00:16:47] leave Uber, raise money, and do something on platform engineering. A classic way that Uber alumni start businesses is, Uber has invested silly amounts of money to build everything custom internally. Everything that you can think of. Our [inaudible 00:17:02] system was custom, our experimentation system, our container, the way we automatically set that up, a lot of the engineering stuff. So a lot of Uber alumni just leave, and whatever they saw there, they just build it for the world to use, because no other company really does what Uber does, because it makes no sense, but a lot of them will pay for.
turns.zh: 所以我的计划是[00:16:47]离开优步，筹集资金，专注于平台工程。优步校友创办企业的经典方式是，优步投入了大量资金内部定制开发所有东西。任何你能想到的功能，我们的[00:17:02]系统是定制的，我们的实验系统、容器、自动化设置等等很多工程方面的东西。所以很多优步校友离开后，无论在优步学到什么，他们都会为全世界打造出来，因为没有其他公司能复制优步的模式，因为这根本不划算，但很多人愿意为此买单。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: That was the plan. But before [inaudible 00:17:22] I wanted to finish a book. I'd been writing this book for, it was coming up to a year, called the Software Engineer's Guidebook, which is just my advice for people to grow professionally in the field. And I figured, all right, let me leave the company, in six months I'll write the book, I'll just use my savings to take a break, and then I'll raise the venture capital. And what happened was, I started to write this book, but I got sidetracked, I started to have fun online in terms of... I was writing on Twitter, on my blog. I accidentally published a book called Building Mobile Apps at Scale. I just did it for a few months.
turns.zh: 这就是计划。但在[00:17:22]离开公司之前，我想先完成一本书。我写这本书快一年了，叫《软件工程师指南》，是我给人们在该领域职业发展提出的建议。我想，好，离开公司后，六个月内写完书，靠储蓄休息一下，然后再筹集风险投资。但结果是，我开始写这本书，却被分心了，在网上玩得很开心，比如在推特、博客上写东西。结果无意中出版了一本叫《大规模开发移动应用》的书。就这样写了几个月。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And the weird thing was that my plan was that I'm going to just not make any money, and this book, Building Mobile Apps at Scale, and another book that I published about tech resumes, I just wrote these in a few months, they started making money. They made about $100,000 in the first year. And I was like, "That's interesting. People are buying my books." And I self-published it through Gumroad or places where I get to keep I think 90% of the revenue, but still, this was really interesting. And I got to the point where, all right, I should now start a startup. I should do fundraising and do all that. And then I asked myself, why do I really want to do that?
turns.zh: 奇怪的是，我的计划本是打算不赚什么钱的。《大规模开发移动应用》这本书，还有我出版的关于技术简历的另一本书，我在几个月内就写完了，结果它们开始赚钱了。第一年就赚了约10万美元。我当时想：“真有意思，居然有人买我的书。”我通过Gumroad等平台自出版，这些平台能让我保留约90%的收入，但即便如此，这还是挺令人兴奋的。后来我意识到，嗯，现在是时候创办一家初创公司了。我应该开始融资之类的操作。然后我问自己：我为什么真的想这么做？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And the answer was two reasons. One is, I love working in small teams at Uber. I'll be honest, I didn't really enjoy being a manager of managers. It felt a bit too abstract. I didn't like being in the meetings, not doing the work. What I really liked is when we had a small team, and we had this really big vision, and it was us against the world. We were like ten of us, and we were just getting stuff done, we were putting out fires, it was so much fun. So that was one of the reasons I wanted to do startup. I was hoping to recreate this feeling.
turns.zh: 答案有两个原因。一个是，我喜欢在Uber的小团队里工作。我说实话，我不太喜欢做管理者的管理者。那种感觉太抽象了。我不喜欢参加那些会议，不做实事。真正让我喜欢的是，当我们有一个小团队，有一个宏大的愿景时，我们就是在与世界对抗。我们大概只有十个人，忙着把事情做好，忙着解决问题，真的很有趣。所以这就是我想创业的原因之一。我希望能重现那种感觉。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And the other thing, honestly, was money. This was in 2021 before the market crashed. Just doing the maths, if you found a company, and I'll be a CEO and the founder, maybe I'll have a co-founder, this becomes a unicorn, by that time we will have raised five rounds of funding or six, I'll be diluted as hell, but I'll still have let's say 5%. 5% of the billion is still $50 million, after you pay taxes [inaudible 00:19:30] I can buy a bunch of stuff that I don't need. And I was asking myself, all right, and then what? And I was like, after I've bought everything that I don't need, I probably want to share what I know with people, do YouTube videos and write books.
turns.zh: 另一个原因，说实话，是钱。这是在2021年市场崩盘之前。算算账吧，如果你创办一家公司，我作为CEO和创始人，可能还有个联合创始人，公司成为独角兽，到那时我们已经融资了五轮或六轮，稀释得厉害，但我可能还持有5%的股份。5%的10亿美元还是5000万美元，扣税后[00:19:30未录]我就能买很多不需要的东西了。然后我问自己，那接下来呢？等我买完所有不需要的东西，我可能就想把自己的知识分享给别人，做YouTube视频，写书了。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And I was thinking to myself, so hold on. I would go off and do this for like ten years, because that's how much you need to plan to do it. I need to stop doing what I'm doing right now, because I would owe it to my investors and my team to not spend all day on the internet writing about stuff. And then I want to do it again. So it's reminding me of the story of this fisherman. There's one that goes [inaudible 00:20:08] there's the same thing of, you work really hard to do what you're doing right now. So I decided, let me just try giving this a go. [inaudible 00:20:14]
turns.zh: 我就在想，等等。这样下去可能要十年时间，因为这就是你需要规划的时间。我现在必须停止做现在这份工作，因为我对投资者和团队有责任，不能整天在网上写东西。然后我又想再试一次。这让我想起那个渔夫的故事。有一个渔夫，他[00:20:08未录]一直在努力做现在这份工作。所以我决定，还是试试看吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, what's the story of the fisherman? I think I know what you're talking about, but... [inaudible 00:20:18]
turns.zh: 等等，渔夫的故事是怎样的？我觉得我知道你说的是哪个故事，但……[00:20:18未录]

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: The story of the fisherman is that, in Mexico, an American businessman sees a fisherman who's just chilling, fishing. And he asks him, "What are you doing all day?" He's like, "I fish for three hours, I hang out with my family, I [inaudible 00:20:32] chill and I sleep in every Saturday and Sunday." He says, "All right, here's what you should be doing. You should fish not three hours, but you should fish five days a week, eight hours a day, sell that fish, turn over a profit, hire more people to do it, then start to be head of all those people, then sell your fishing company." He's like, "Okay. And then what?" "And then you can actually buy an island, and you can just fish for three hours, you can sleep in on Saturdays and sleep on Sundays."
turns.zh: 渔夫的故事是这样的：在墨西哥，一位美国商人看到一个渔夫正在悠闲地钓鱼。他问：“你每天都做什么？” 渔夫回答：“我钓三个小时鱼，陪家人玩，[00:20:32的背景音]休息休息，然后周六周日睡懒觉。” 商人说：“好吧，我来给你建议。你不应该只钓三个小时鱼，而应该每周工作五天，每天八小时，把鱼卖掉赚点钱，再雇人帮你，然后成为这些人的老板，最后卖掉你的渔业公司。” 渔夫问：“然后呢？” 商人回答：“然后你就能买个小岛，继续钓三个小时鱼，周六周日睡懒觉了。”

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So I was thinking, look, I have savings. I don't have huge, but I have it for... I can still take a risk. So let me take a risk on writing. And I was thinking originally of just spending more time to finish my book. But what I didn't like about books, even though I was making money, is they're really... It's hard to predict if you're going to be making a living, or there's some people who actually like this excitement, but I didn't like it. I didn't know if today I'm going to be making like 50 bucks or 10 bucks or 300 bucks. So I was like, interesting. There's these paid newsletters which I've been thinking about, and you were one of the few people who shared some of your early numbers, and I figured this could be interesting, because it's recurring revenue.
turns.zh: 于是我就在想，看吧，我有存款。虽然不算多，但至少能承担风险。所以我决定在写作上冒险一下。最初我只想多花点时间完成我的书，但即便能赚钱，写书这事也太不稳定了。我不知道今天能赚50美元、10美元还是300美元。所以我觉得有意思的是那些付费订阅的新闻letter，我一直在考虑做这个，而你是最早分享早期数据的人之一。我觉得这可能挺不错的，因为有固定收入。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And the only reason I was really hesitant to start a paid newsletter, I was thinking about doing so for at least 6 to 12 months, is I was worried about writing every single week something really, really worthwhile reading, and it's a lot of work. But then I looked back and I saw that I wrote three books. [inaudible 00:21:58] I told you I wrote two books, but there was a third one that I also published in a year, and I was like, I'm pretty sure I can write. So for two weeks I collected ideas of what I would write about, and I had this super long list. So I was like, okay, ideas also check.
turns.zh: 唯一让我犹豫是否要做付费新闻letter的原因，是我担心每周都要写出真正值得一读的深度内容，这太耗费精力了。但回头看，我写了三本书。[00:21:58的背景音]我跟你说过我写了两本书，但还有第三本，也是我在一年内出版的。我觉得自己肯定能写作。所以过去两周，我收集了写作灵感，有个超长的清单。所以我想，好吧，这个点子也不错。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And then I just said, screw it, I'm going to take a risk. It's a bit of a more professional risk, and maybe a financial one as well. I'll announce that I'm going to start a paid newsletter. Every week, I'm going to write something really in depth about software engineering. It's going to start next week. And I told myself that I'll... I told my wife as well that I'll do this for six months, and I'll see what happens. If there's traction, it's great. I might have found myself a new job, basically. If not, I'll just refund people. Everyone who bought an annual subscription... I didn't tell this to people, obviously, but for six months I'm going to give it my all. It's basically like a startup. So I told her and my family that it's going to be a lot of work and I might not be around as much, and they supported me, and I took a plunge. I took a big breath and started off. And that's how it went from leaving Uber to starting a venture funded startup to starting to write full time.
turns.zh: 然后我就想，管他呢，冒险一把。这算个比较专业的冒险，可能还有经济风险。我要宣布要开个付费新闻letter。每周我会写一篇关于软件工程的深度文章。下周就开始。我告诉自己，要坚持六个月，看看结果如何。如果反响不错，可能就找到新工作了。如果不行，就退款给所有买年度订阅的人。当然我没跟别人说过，但这六个月我会全力以赴。这就像创业一样。所以我告诉家人和妻子，这会很忙，可能陪他们少了，但他们支持我，我就豁出去了。深吸一口气，开始行动了。这就是从离开Uber到创办风投支持的创业公司，再到全职写作的转变过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And we're going to talk about what advice you have for folks that are thinking about starting something like this at the end. What was the period between leaving Uber and starting the newsletter?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后我们会聊聊你对那些想尝试类似事业的人有什么建议。从离开Uber到开通新闻letter这段时间有多久？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: It was pretty much a year, a little bit less than a year. Might have been like ten months or so, but it was a year from when I decided to leave Uber. So Uber did layoffs in April, and it was really stressful. It was the first time I... I didn't lay anyone off, but people on my team were laid off. I wasn't told who's going to be laid off. It was just really stressful. It's weird, in the sense that the people who were let go, obviously worse for them, but I still felt terrible, and I just didn't feel very good about it. I think this was the breaking point. This was the point where I realized that it's not a family, which is weird because it never was, but it kind of felt family-like, but it's just a corporate, and I'm just a number, and this could happen to me, I guess. So I think I lost my sense of the trust in the system, that it'll take care of me, because I saw some of my colleagues who were really good professionals, I'd argue they were better software engineers and managers than me, they got let go because they were in the wrong team.
turns.zh: 差不多有一年，比一年稍微短一点。可能有十个月左右，但从我决定离开优步那天起，就已经过去了一年。优步在四月份裁员，那段时间压力非常大。那是我第一次……我没有裁掉任何人，但我团队里有人被裁掉了。他们没有告诉我谁会被裁掉。压力真的很大。这很奇怪，被裁掉的人显然更遭，但我还是感觉很糟糕，对此心里很不好受。我觉得那是崩溃的时刻。就在那时，我意识到这根本不是一个大家庭，尽管它曾被描绘成家庭般的组织，但本质上还是一家公司，而我只是个数字，随时可能被裁掉。我想我对这个系统失去了信任，认为它会照顾我，因为我看到一些同事，他们都是非常优秀的专业人士——我敢说他们比我更出色的软件工程师和管理者，却因为身处错误的团队而被裁掉。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So this was April, and in July I went to a holiday, and two weeks in, I just realized I need to leave. And I really had the urge to do somewhere where I'm in charge. And if you're a manager listening to this, you might relate to this. If you're an engineer listening to this, maybe just shut your ears or you'll figure it out eventually. But when I was promoted into management... It wasn't promoting into it, because it was a side step, I didn't get [inaudible 00:24:34] or anything, but it still feels a promotion. They only promote the people who are... Only let people transition who are considered pretty good. I felt this would be a big deal. I'm now a manager. What no one told me is, yes I was a manager, but I was a middle manager. I didn't have too much authority. I didn't even have budget for my team. Someone was underpaid and I couldn't do anything except complain for HR for six months and hope that they'd do something.
turns.zh: 四月份的事，七月份我去度假，两周后突然意识到自己必须离开了。我真的很想去一个能让我当老板的地方。如果你是一位正在听节目的管理者，或许能感同身受。如果你是一位工程师，可能只需屏蔽这段内容，因为最终你总会明白的。但当我晋升到管理层时……这算不上晋升，因为只是横向调动，没有获得任何头衔或晋升机会，但在别人眼中依然是晋升。他们只晋升那些被认为相当优秀的人。我觉得这事意义重大。我现在是经理了，但没人告诉我，尽管我是经理，却只是中层管理者。没有太多权力。甚至连团队预算都没有。有人工资过低，我只能向人力资源部门抱怨六个月，却始终得不到解决。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So it was pretty frustrating, because I didn't feel in charge in the sense that I didn't have decision making [inaudible 00:25:02]. And the reason I wanted to do a startup is, I decided I liked being a manager, but I did not how I was not in charge and I couldn't take corporate [inaudible 00:25:12] telling us to do stuff, and then we were telling them no [inaudible 00:25:16] I don't want to do that with my people. So I decided for next job, I could be doing this, but instead I'd like to be in charge. So I'd like to be a founder or someone who's high up, so that I can actually take full responsibility for the things that I want to do or I don't want to do. The short of it is, I decided to leave in July. We have longer notice periods in Europe, so I served a longer notice period, and then left. But it was a year after the decision.
turns.zh: 所以压力很大，因为我没有决策权……（00:25:02语音不清）。所以我想做创业公司的初衷是，我决定自己喜欢做管理者，但我不明白自己为何没有掌控权，不能对公司要求做事的指令说“不”（00:25:16语音不清）。我不想对自己的团队这样做。所以我决定下份工作要能做主。于是我想成为创始人或高层，这样我才能对想做或不想做的事全权负责。简而言之，我七月决定离开。欧洲的离职通知期较长，所以我履行了较长的通知期后离开了。但从决定离开到实际离开已经过去了一年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about what your life is like these days, writing a newsletter full time. People might be listening and be like, "Man, $300,000 for writing an email a couple times a week, that's pretty sweet." So I want to talk about the good and the bad of this life. So maybe to start, how many posts are you putting out a week?
turns.zh: 我们来聊聊你现在的生活吧，全职写通讯稿。听众可能会想：“哇，每周写几封邮件就能赚30万美元，真是太棒了。”所以我想聊聊这种生活的好与坏。或许先从你每周发布的帖子数量说起？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I started the newsletter saying I'm going to post once a week. You'll have one pinned up post. And I started to do that, but interesting enough, eventually I upped it to two, so I now promise people two posts a week. There's more in depth and more timeless posts about some software engineering topic on Tuesdays, and there's something that's called the scoop, something a bit more timely, where I reflect or analyze what's going on in the market, interesting stuff I'm hearing. And every now and then there's a bonus post. So I'll say two on average, but the second one came a lot later. But initially in the first few months I was like, I have this one post per week, and it needs to be good.
turns.zh: 我最初在发送通讯时说，我打算每周发布一篇文章。你们会看到一篇置顶帖。我一开始确实做到了，但有趣的是，最终我把频率提高到了两篇，所以现在我向读者承诺每周发布两篇内容。每周二会有更深入、更具永久价值的软件工程主题文章，而每周三则会发布一篇名为"独家报道"的专栏，内容更具时效性——我会反思或分析市场动态，以及听到的有趣消息。偶尔还会有额外的加更内容。所以平均来说我每周发布两篇，但第二篇通常发布得比较晚。不过最初的几个月，我还是坚持每周一篇，而且必须保证质量。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And it was interesting, because you would think writing a post a week is not a big deal. It's easy. As you said, let's say you're making 300K just writing one post a week. But it actually was pretty stressful in the beginning, because it turns out to write that post, it takes at least a few days or sometimes even longer. Sometimes it takes a week or two for me to research in terms of talking with people. I chose topics that are not covered, because why would people pay for something that is out there already or well known? Then I need to write [inaudible 00:27:10] a first draft. I get some feedback from people who I trust often, not always, but I often do. And then there's an editing phase where I work with an editor who helps make sure that it's just correct. And all these things add up. Even if I only spend a day researching the stuff, it's a day researching, then I have a draft on day two. Day three I get feedback, on day four it's editing, it's almost a whole week.
turns.zh: 这很有意思，因为你可能会觉得每周写一篇文章没什么大不了的。很简单。正如你所说，如果你每周写一篇文章就能赚30万美元。但一开始确实压力很大，因为写一篇文章至少需要几天时间，有时甚至更久。有时我需要花一两周时间做调研，采访相关人士。我选择那些未被充分报道的主题，因为如果人们已经了解或熟知某个领域的内容，又何必为此付费呢？然后我要写初稿。我会经常征求信任的人的反馈意见，虽然不总是这样，但确实经常这样。接下来是编辑阶段，我会和编辑合作，确保内容准确无误。所有这些步骤加起来很耗时。即使我只花一天时间研究素材，第二天写初稿，第三天收集反馈，第四天编辑，整个过程几乎要一周时间。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So I was working on parallel things at the same time, and I was often running against the deadline, I was barely finishing it, which is not what I was expecting initially. The first few months I feel was a bit more stressed, but again, the good thing is I cleared my calendar, so I said I'm not talking with anyone, I'm just doing this. So in that sense it was good. But the one thing I realized, if you look at any journalists who's doing stuff full time, and they're writing, not these clickbait articles, but actually in depth. You look at the Washington Post or New York Times, search for their name, and look up the articles that they write, and they're going to be longer articles. They have like one a month. Seriously. You look at the investigative journalist, they might even have less. And they have a bit of a different level, they have to check with legal and all those things, but my editor is a journalist, so he was actually telling me, even back then, "You actually write a lot of original stuff," because a lot of my emails are about five, 6,000 words, which is considered very long.
turns.zh: 所以我同时处理多项任务，经常赶在截止日期前完成任务，这与我最初的预期大不相同。最初的几个月压力更大，但好在我清理了日程安排，告诉自己不与任何人交谈，只专注于这项工作。从这个角度来看还是不错的。但我意识到，如果你观察那些全职从事新闻工作的记者，他们写的都是深度报道，比如《华盛顿邮报》或《纽约时报》，你搜索他们的名字，查看他们撰写的文章，通常都是长篇大论。他们每月可能只写一篇文章。说真的，调查记者可能写得更少。他们需要面对法律审查等各种复杂问题，但我的编辑也是记者，所以他甚至在那时就对我说：“你其实写了很多原创内容。”因为我的很多邮件都有五六千字，这被认为是长篇内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. When you said that people listening might be like, one post a week is easy, I think most people are the opposite. They're just like, I can't write anything. I don't have time for any writing. How can you ever write one good thing a week? So I think there's both sides to it. And it's cool that you shared the process. Do you have a specific cadence per post? It's like Monday draft, Tuesday review, Wednesday editor. Is that how you work?
turns.zh: 是的。你说听众可能会觉得每周一篇很容易，我觉得大多数人的看法恰恰相反。他们会觉得自己什么都写不出来，没有时间写作。怎么能每周写出一篇好文章呢？所以这件事有利有弊。很高兴你能分享这个过程。每篇文章你有特定的创作节奏吗？比如周一写初稿，周二校对，周三交给编辑？你是这样工作的吗？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I write every post over multiple weeks, most of them. Some of them I might be able to write faster, but what I now have is, nowadays I actually write two articles. So I have the Thursday that is the scoop, which actually is a lot easier for me to write, interestingly enough. And my cadence is, on Monday I finish up the last of the post that goes out on Tuesday. It's just small edits, but it's already done pretty much, so it's just a few small tweaks, and maybe I have some feedback coming in. On Tuesday, I publish this post, and I do some free writing. I write about some other ideas that I have that's going to be future posts. On Wednesday, it's my free day in between, where I... It's interesting, because what I feel is, when I don't have pressure, I tend to not do much stuff, which might just... My mind's saying, "You just need to chill." Maybe that's it.
turns.zh: 我每篇文章都是分几周写的，大多数都是这样。有些文章或许能写得更快，但现在的情况是，我现在每天要写两篇文章。周四的那篇是头条新闻，写起来相对容易得多，有趣的是。我的写作节奏是，周一完成周二发布的最后一篇文章。只是做些微调，但基本已经完成，所以只需要做些小修改，或许还会有反馈意见。周二发布这篇文章后，再进行自由写作，写一些未来要发布的其他想法。周三是中间的休息日，可以……有趣的是，我发现当没有压力时，自己往往什么都不做，可能只是……大脑在说：“你只需要放松。”也许就是这样。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: But one thing I miss from the corporate world... And if you're listening and you're in a job and you're thinking, "Gergely's job is so amazing," one thing that I liked and I really miss about working at Uber is, I actually had a schedule. This is weird, I hated it back then, but I needed to do these things, and whenever you have a pressure, you do it. And this works with my newsletter. I put in the second newsletter I think to have a bit more pressure. Because the second part of Wednesday, I'm already starting to write my Thursday newsletter. On Thursday, I write that Thursday newsletter, and on Friday I'm now writing the next newsletter for Tuesday. So almost every day except for Wednesday, I have a strong pressure to write. Which when people ask, "Gergely, how do you write so much?" Because I did the maths, and I wrote four or five books' worth of content just last year. It's because I have these deadlines, and as you said, I also know that thousands of people are paying me, they have expectations of me.
turns.zh: 但有一点让我怀念起职场生活……如果你正在听，正在工作，心里想“格尔吉的工作太棒了”，让我真正怀念优步工作的就是，公司有严格的日程安排。说来奇怪，当时我讨厌这种安排，但不得不按时完成任务。一旦有压力，就会促使你行动起来。这也适用于我的新闻通讯。我觉得第二期通讯的推出，是我给自己施加更大压力的结果。因为周三的下半段，我已经开始写周四的通讯了。周四写完周四的通讯后，周五就开始写周二的下期通讯。所以除了周三，几乎每天我都承受着写作的巨大压力。当人们问：“格尔吉，你怎么写这么多东西？”我会说，是因为我有截止日期。正如你所说，我也知道有成千上万的人在期待我的内容。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And so this is how it's done. If you want to write a book, the easiest way is go to a publisher and sign a contract, not because of the money. In software engineering, you're not going to get much [inaudible 00:30:57] $5,000 or something like that. That's what I was offered initially. But it's the pressure. You absolutely should go to a publisher or have some external... Someone to hold you accountable, and then you'll get it done. And I'll let you in on another secret, or not so secret.
turns.zh: 这就是成功的秘诀。如果你想写本书，最简单的方法就是找出版社签约合同，不是因为钱。在软件工程领域，你赚不了多少钱[00:30:57不可听清]，5000美元之类的。这就是最初给我的报价。但关键在于压力。你绝对应该找出版社或寻求外部监督，这样才能完成任务。我再透露个小秘密，或者说不算秘密。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do tell.
turns.zh: 说吧。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: In my mind, when I started newsletter a year ago in this crossroads, I want to write this book, which I think will be a great book, the Software Engineer's Guidebook, I feel it'll be my summary of my last ten years of what I have to share as advice, but I was worried that it's just a big project that's just going to take months, and I'll lose motivation midway.
turns.zh: 在我一年前开始写通讯、处于十字路口的时候，我想写这本书，我觉得会是一本很棒的书，《软件工程师指南》，我觉得这会是我过去十年经验的总结，分享一些建议，但我担心这是一个大项目，耗时数月，而且中途会失去动力。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And partially, I went down the newsletter route because I liked how every week I would have to write something, and I had this sneaky idea of, what if I wrote this book where I write some posts that will be part of the book, and then the book will just come together partially. And I've kind of been doing that. I haven't been telling people, but some of the posts are going to be... Not exactly, but the idea is that I have this chapter, and I have this list, have I written about this topic in the newsletter? And you know where I got this idea from? There's the book The Three Musketeers, from Alexander Dumas [inaudible 00:32:12]. And do you know how it was written?
turns.zh: 部分原因，我选择了写通讯的路线，因为我喜欢每周都要写点东西的感觉。我还有个偷偷的想法：如果我写这本书时，先写一些会成为书中内容的帖子，然后再把这些帖子逐渐整合成书，怎么样？我一直在这么做，虽然没告诉别人，但有些帖子确实会被收录进书里……不完全一样，但思路是这样的：我有一个章节，列了一个清单，我在通讯里写过这个主题吗？你知道我这个想法的灵感来自哪里吗？是大仲马的《三剑客》！你知道它是怎么写的吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't.
turns.zh: 我不知道。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So he wrote the book for a magazine. He was apparently just low on money, and he started to write for this magazine who told them, "All right, we need you to write something that our readers will want, so that they will buy the magazine." I think he was getting a cut of some sales or something. So he needs to write in a way that was interesting, and then cut it off in a way that people would come back and buy the next one. And he wrote a whole book, and that book, when I read it, it's really long, and I was like, hold on, if he could do this, then this is a good strategy. He was writing it because he just needed the money. That's all. And then he wrote a really good book on the way.
turns.zh: 所以他为一本杂志写书。显然他当时资金短缺，就开始为这本杂志写稿。杂志方对他说：“好吧，我们需要你写读者感兴趣的内容，这样他们才会买杂志。”我记得他能从销售中分成什么的。所以他必须写得有趣，又要留个悬念，让读者期待下一期。最后他写成了一整本书，我读的时候，发现它篇幅很长，我当时就想，等等，如果他能做到这样，那这真是个好策略。他写这本书就是为了赚钱，仅此而已。但最后他还是写出了一本很棒的书。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So one big learning for me from newsletters then... I would argue that you can use this not just for newsletters, but any business that you do. If you're going to go out and start a new business, you'll probably have some ideas. And it's not just going to be a newsletter, it's going to be a bunch of other things. If you put in ways that you have to do certain things, put in constraints for the things that you need to do, and then you're going to do that.
turns.zh: 所以从通讯中学到的一个重要经验……我认为这个方法不仅适用于通讯，也适用于任何创业项目。如果你要创业，肯定会有一些想法。不会只写通讯，可能还涉及其他方面。如果你设定一些必须完成的任务，为需要做的事情设定限制条件，那么你就能做到。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Without that, when you're on your own, when you're entrepreneur, I was a great... I think I was a really diligent employee. I always tried to get my work done, show up on time, I tried to meet all expectations. But what I noticed is, when I started to work for myself, it just went out the window. Almost 15 years of being this star employee who really wants to do well, I found myself upset at myself for not... Just wasting my day. But I fixed it by telling people, "You're going to get this every week," and now I have to do it. I just have no choice.
turns.zh: 否则，当你独自创业时，就会一团乱麻。我曾是个很勤奋的员工，总能按时完成工作，满足所有要求。但创业后，情况完全变了。在做了15年尽职尽责的员工后，突然发现自己连最基本的自律都做不到，整天虚度光阴。不过我改正了这个问题，告诉别人“每周都要交稿”，现在我不得不按时完成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Vanta, helping you streamline your security compliance to accelerate growth. If your business stores any data in the cloud, then you've likely been asked or you're going to be asked about your SOC 2 compliance. SOC 2 is a way to prove your company's taking proper security measures to protect customer data, and builds trust with customers and partners, especially those with serious security requirements. Also, if you want to sell to the enterprise, proving security is essential. SOC 2 can either open the door for bigger and better deals, or it can put your business on hold. turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Yeah. turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Yeah. So there is definitely going to be extensions that you can use, and on this podcast we'll have a variety of people. I compensate for that by working in a shared workspace, a shared office, which is a techy workspace. So everyone needs to work in tech. So I actually get to say hi to people and have a little small talk.
turns.zh: 很显然，孤独感是其中之一。我确实很怀念……我在优步的团队非常棒，那不仅仅是一个团队，更是一群志同道合的伙伴。我很喜欢……每个人对远程工作的看法各不相同。我其实不太喜欢远程工作，因为我喜欢与人交流。我属于比较外向的类型，喜欢走到咖啡站和同事聊天，或者午餐时坐在别人旁边闲聊。不过有时候这也挺烦人的，因为我需要完成工作，但大多数时候我对远程工作的怀念远超其带来的不便。因此，我选择在共享办公空间工作，和其他科技行业从业者一起交流，这样就能和大家打招呼，聊聊天了。

turns.en: So there's that part, but there's a lot of external validation, so whenever looking at your subscriber numbers, which brings a bunch of stress that I didn't expect.
