One is, with a paid newsletter especially, but even with a sponsored newsletter, you basically have to get something awesome out every week, in theory for the rest of your life. People are buying an annual plan every day, so that means at least a year you have to write something awesome, if you want to stop. But it's hard to stop, because as you pointed out, the income is very meaningful, and that's a hard thing to give up. And so I'm not sure exactly the exit path that exists for us, where we might have to keep writing something awesome for the rest of our life, but I imagine something will emerge and we'll think of something else that we could do.
turns.zh: 实际上我还想问问你这方面的问题，但我还要补充几点我认为这种生活方式的主要弊端，毕竟生活并非处处美好。首先，特别是对于付费订阅通讯而言，即便是有赞助商支持的通讯，你也基本得每周产出高质量内容——理论上这要持续一辈子才行。如果你想停业，人们每天都在购买年度订阅计划，这意味着至少一年内你必须持续创作优质内容。但要停业其实很难，因为正如你所指出的，这份收入意义非凡，要放弃实在太难了。所以我不确定我们有怎样的退出路径——可能得一辈子持续创作优质内容，但我相信总会有新的机遇出现，我们会找到别的出路。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Yeah. And it's a really good example, because for a lot of companies, and I assume a lot of listeners are working in tech, typical thing is you work hard, you build equity at a company or you build the value of the company, and then you can sell that company, and then you can have an exit and you can do whatever. For what we're doing, it's really tied to us. So however much or little my newsletter will make, it'll have a value let's say four or five times the annual revenue as a business, but you cannot really sell it like that and you cannot really walk away.
turns.zh: 是啊。这是个很好的例子，因为对很多公司而言——我猜听众中很多人都在科技行业工作——典型的模式是努力工作，积累公司股权或提升公司价值，然后出售公司，获得退出机会，随后就可以自由支配了。但对我们而言，情况与此截然不同。无论我们的通讯能赚多少钱，它作为业务的价值可能达到年收入的四五倍，但你无法真正将其出售，也无法全身而退。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So that makes it unique, it makes it harder to compete with, which is cool, but it does not create that much of an exit path unless you start to build a company around it, build an organization that can run without you, for example. This is what a lot of book publishing companies... So basically you build a publishing company where you start to hire people, who start to write some of the articles initially, and then later more of them, but it's not a one-person newsletter any more. Or you keep doing this, until you either stop and then the revenue stops, or you might be able to sell it, but at really under value.
turns.zh: 这使我们独具特色，也更难与他人竞争，这固然不错，但除非你围绕它组建一家公司——比如建立一个无需你亲自管理就能运转的组织——否则很难找到退出路径。许多图书出版公司就是这么做的。基本上，就是组建一家出版公司，起初雇人撰写部分文章，后来逐渐增加人手，但这不再是单人运营的通讯了。要么你一直坚持下去，直到收入停滞，要么可能以极低价格出售公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I really don't want to manage people. I don't want to have employees. And so building a media company with writers, that doesn't sound too fun, but maybe that's where this goes. That is one route, for sure. The other downside I'll just add is the fact that you have to write something awesome every week, it's hard to take meaningful time off, because if you stop producing great stuff, people leave. And I invented this PTO policy for myself where I take four weeks a year off, where I don't do a newsletter, but that means I can't take more than a week off usually [inaudible 00:48:58] weeks in a row, I don't know, people probably won't care, but it feels like things start to not go great if I just don't keep producing great stuff. So that's another downside, just [inaudible 00:49:08] topic.
turns.zh: 是啊。我真的不想管理员工。我不想雇人。所以组建一家有撰稿人的媒体公司听起来不太有趣，但也许这就是我们的发展方向。这肯定是一条路径。另一个弊端是每周都得产出高质量内容，很难抽出有意义的休假时间，因为一旦停止优质内容输出，用户就会流失。我为自己制定了四周年假政策，期间不发通讯，但这意味着我通常不能连续休假超过一周[00:48:58不清]，可能人们不会在意，但如果我持续不了优质内容，业务就会下滑。这就是另一个弊端，回到[00:49:08不清]话题。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Yeah. But a lot [inaudible 00:49:11] very early. So I think the whole concept of paying users is new, so I think we're going to do a lot of experimentation. And also a lot of it, I think you need to figure out what your needs are. So in the first year, I did not take a holiday in terms of... Or even when I [inaudible 00:49:25] I was writing, and it caused a bit of friction with my family. And now I'm solving it in a different way, so I am planning to take more time off now, and I'm doing it by working ahead with some of the less time sensitive things. But it is tough.
turns.zh: 是的。但很多时候（听不清 00:49:11）太早了。所以我认为向用户收费这个概念还是很新的，我们需要做很多尝试。还有很多时候，你得先明确自己的需求。第一年的时候，我根本没放假……甚至当我（听不清 00:49:25）写作时，和家人产生了不少矛盾。现在我换了种方式解决问题——提前处理一些不那么紧急的事务，这样就能腾出更多时间休息。但这确实很难。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So a downside we haven't mentioned, but I'm just going to call it out, is holiday. The great thing at... I never felt... Well, I felt a little guilty sometimes taking holiday, but when I want a holiday, I took it off. When I had my son born, at Uber, they gave me a four month paid holiday. I took the whole four months, I just logged off. It was great. It wasn't my company. I was still getting stock. The stock price was independent of mostly what I was doing, just being honest. And that was really, really good. So this might be true, by the way, if you start any business, especially while it's just yourself, it's hard to turn off. And I think most people don't mind, I don't mind, but it gets to you. We should be conscious about burnout as a whole. So you need to solve for that, and I'm starting to solve for that as well.
turns.zh: 还有个我们没提到的弊端，不过我还是要说出来，那就是休假。优步公司给我的四个月带薪产假真是太棒了。我休了整整四个月，完全不上班。这段时光很棒。当时公司不归我管，但我还能领股票。说实话，那时的股票价格基本不受我个人表现影响。这真是太好了。所以如果你创业，尤其是独自创业，真的很难切断工作和生活的界限。我觉得大多数人都能接受，我自己也不介意，但这确实会让人精疲力竭。我们应该时刻警惕职业倦怠的问题。所以你得想办法应对，我现在也正在这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. Enough about the downsides. Overall, it's pretty amazing making hundreds of thousands of dollars writing an email once a week/twice a week. So just to wrap up on that, I'm curious, where do you think this goes long term for you? And then I want to talk about just what it takes to be successful, but before there, do you think this goes long term?
turns.zh: 是的。好的，关于弊端就说到这儿。总的来说，每周写一封/两封邮件就能赚几十万美元，这真是太棒了。最后再问问你，你觉得这项业务未来能发展成什么样？然后我想聊聊成功的要素，但在那之前，你觉得这项业务的长期前景如何？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I stopped making long term plans, because three years ago you would've asked me what I wanted to do, and I was like, "I want to be, I don't know, a manager of managers." And then I became one. And then [inaudible 00:51:01] what is my dream? I would've been like, "It's a stretch, but maybe I want to be a site lead." And I didn't become one per se, but I never thought of writing a newsletter, or now writing a successful newsletter. So I'm going with the flow. I'm seeing this less, by the way, as a newsletter or creator, or creator economy as people like to see it. I see this as a business, and I'm trying to put on that business hat. I'm building a one-person business. I want to make it sustainable, I want to make it successful, and I find that this thinking really helps me detach as well. I can actually enjoy my weekends as opposed to thinking, "I need to write this, or I need to write that." So I also want to make it work for me.
turns.zh: 我已经不做长期规划了。三年前要是有人问我想做什么，我可能会说“我要当个管理者的管理者”。结果我真成了一个管理者。但（听不清 00:51:01）我的梦想是什么？我可能会说“这有点不切实际，但或许我想当站点负责人”。虽然我没当上，但我从没想过写通讯，或者现在成功运营通讯。所以我顺其自然。说实话，我不把这看作通讯或创作者经济（就像人们常说的那样），而是把它当作一门生意，我正努力以商业思维去经营。我在打造一个一人公司。我想让它可持续发展、取得成功，而且我发现这种思维方式真的能帮助我抽离出来。现在我能真正享受周末了，而不是总想着“我得写这个、写那个”。所以我也要让它为我服务。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And I'm not married to the idea of, it always needs to be a newsletter, et cetera. Right now it is, but where I see us going is, I'll keep building the business, I'll keep playing to my strength, which is I love talking with people, I love writing [inaudible 00:51:56] I love software engineering. So this is a great format, but over time it might shift. So I'm keeping my options open. And what I've learned from this journey is, you need to create time for that spark to come. So one of my goals for next few years is to not spend 50 hours a week on a newsletter, which I'm doing right now, but spend 20, and then maybe take a few weeks off and have that spark come. Because the reality is, this newsletter only came because I gave myself six months of unpaid... I'm not going for work, I didn't ask for any LinkedIn emails. And the idea came and the inspiration came and the motivation came.
turns.zh: 还有，我对新闻通讯的形式并没有太执着，不一定非得一直保持这个模式。现在是这样，但未来可能会调整。所以我会保持开放的心态。通过这次经历，我明白了要为灵感的迸发留出时间。因此，未来几年的目标就是不再每周花50个小时在新闻通讯上——我现在就是这样做的，但可能会改成每周20个小时，然后休息几周，让灵感自然涌现。毕竟这个新闻通讯之所以能成功，是因为我给自己六个月无偿假期——我不是去找工作，也没去收集领英邮箱——灵感就是这样来的，动力就是这样来的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of similarities with my approach. I don't think too far long term. I have no idea what's going to happen. I just take it to... I see where pull is coming from, and if it feels like an interesting opportunity and something that I'd be excited to work on, I explore it, like the podcast for example. And on that point, I will say, once you find that you can spend maybe 20 hours on a newsletter, I guarantee you'll find more work to fill that gap, because that's what I've been doing.
turns.zh: 我的方法和他有很多相似之处。我不做长远规划，不知道未来会怎样。只是顺势而为，看看哪里有吸引力，如果觉得有趣、值得投入，就去探索。比如播客项目。说到这，我想说，一旦你发现自己每周能花20小时做新闻通讯，我保证你会找到更多事情来填补空闲时间，因为我现在就是这样做的。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Yeah. And one last thing to touch on, you said something really important [inaudible 00:53:06] pull, and I want to double down on that. One of the biggest, best things about doing what we do when you're in charge of your time is, you can double down on pulls. So [inaudible 00:53:18] Uber, like I said, my plan was, I'll write this book for six months. Two months in, I just put a draft [inaudible 00:53:24] a really long blog post about mobile engineering, and I got a ton of messages, a lot. I usually used to get like three or four messages on Twitter per day. I got 20 in an hour, people saying, "Can I read the draft?" And I was like, that's interesting. I just felt this pull, of this huge interest of people caring about this. It was this really long blog post about mobile engineering at scale, and someone suggested on a private message, "You could probably turn this into a ebook." And I was like, that's a good idea, because it's a really long blog post. So I said, "It's going to be an ebook, and it'll be pay what you want." And then people started to buy it. And I was like, that's interesting.
turns.zh: 是的。最后再强调一点，你提到的一个关键点——被动吸引力（pull），我想再强调一下。当你能掌控自己的时间时，被动吸引力就是最大的优势之一。所以[音频中断00:53:06]优步项目，我原本计划用六个月写这本书。两个月后，刚写了个长篇博客，讲移动工程的，结果收到大量留言。通常我每天在推特上收到三四条消息，这次一小时内就收到20条，人们问“能看初稿吗？”我觉得很有意思，感觉到这种被动吸引力——大家对这个话题很感兴趣。这篇长博客讲大规模移动工程，有个私信建议“可以写成电子书”。我觉得不错，毕竟篇幅太长了。于是我决定做成电子书，采用“随你付”模式。结果大家开始购买，我觉得很有趣。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So I didn't have much else to do, so I was able to double down. I said, for the next two months, I'm going to write this book, because it seems there's an interest in it. And [inaudible 00:54:07] I turned it into a book that was free for two months, but I got sponsorship. The point was, I was able to double down on this pull. And same thing with the newsletter. So we're going to talk about how I got the first few thousand subscribers, but the point was, I was able to double down on something that I felt like, this is super interesting, I never expected that people would care about building a large mobile app, more than a few hundred people. Turns out they do. Thousands do.
turns.zh: 当时我没什么其他事做，所以能全力投入。接下来两个月，我专心写书，因为感觉大家有兴趣。[音频中断00:54:07]最后免费开放两个月，还收到了赞助。关键是，我能全力投入到这种被动吸引力中去。新闻通讯也是如此。我们会讲讲我是如何获得最初几千订阅用户的，但重点是，我能全力投入到自己觉得超级有趣的事情中。我从没想过会有几百人关心如何开发大型移动应用，结果成千上万的人感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually jump to that. Let's talk about just how to get started, for folks that are like, "This is cool. I want to do a newsletter." Let's talk about just how you got started briefly, and then what you think it takes to be successful in the life of a newsletter person. So how'd you actually get your first thousand subscribers?
turns.zh: 咱们直接进入正题吧。对于那些心想“这太棒了，我也想做个新闻通讯”的人，让我们先简单聊聊如何起步。再谈谈你如何快速入门，以及在做新闻通讯这份事业中取得成功需要具备哪些条件。那么，你究竟是如何获得首批1000名订阅者的呢？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I'll tell the story that is kind of true, and people will think it's amazing, and also the real deal behind it.
turns.zh: 我要讲一个真实的故事，人们会觉得很惊奇，同时这也是背后的真实秘诀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I announced my newsletter, I told people, "I'm going to go full time on this." I had maybe 10,000 Twitter followers and, I don't know, maybe 1,000 on LinkedIn or something that. And people started signing up the next day. I had 100 subscribers in the first day before I published anything. And within six weeks, when I published my [inaudible 00:55:15] I had 1,000 paid subscribers. And this sounds like a fairytale. And if you do this, I guarantee you're not going to get the same results. In fact, you'll probably see way smaller numbers.
turns.zh: 我宣布了我的新闻通讯，告诉大家：“我要全职投入这项事业。”当时我大概有1万名推特粉丝，领英上的粉丝可能1000左右。结果第二天就开始有人订阅了。在发布第一篇文章前，我首日就收获了100名付费订阅者。六周后，当我发布我的[00:55:15听不清]时，我已经有1000名付费订阅者了。这听起来像个童话故事。但如果你照搬我的做法，保证不会得到同样的结果。事实上，你很可能只会看到微不足道的数据。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: What I didn't tell is that there was at least six years of accidental work behind this. I started a blog six years before... Actually, I've always been blogging since I graduated. I had this personal blog where I just published all sorts of random things about software engineering, but it was really... Sometimes it was about an app that I published, sometimes it was a problem that I came across. It was is all over the place. And I got fed up with this, the blog wasn't going anywhere, and I was just writing for myself, by the way, but I didn't how it was just all over the place.
turns.zh: 我没提的是，这背后至少有六年的不经意的努力。六年前我开了一个博客……实际上，我从大学毕业后就一直在写博客。我有个个人博客，里面随意发布各种关于软件工程的内容，但内容非常零散。有时是关于我发布的应用，有时是遇到的难题。总之内容很杂乱。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And I said, "I'm going to start a blog, it'll be about software engineering and I'll call it The Pragmatic Engineer." I bought the domain, and I read this blog post from Jeff Atwood, who's the founder of Stack Overflow, and back in 2010, or I think in 2007 when I was still in college, he had the most popular blog on the internet for software engineers. It was called Coding Horror, and all the software engineers I knew read it and were drinking it. It was next level wisdom every single week, twice [inaudible 00:56:26] a week. You read it as well?
turns.zh: 于是我决定开一个博客，主题是软件工程，取名为《务实工程师》。我买了域名，还读了Stack Overflow创始人杰夫·阿特伍德的一篇博文。2010年左右，我还在上大学时，他在网上开设了最受欢迎的软件工程博客，叫《Coding Horror》。我认识的所有软件工程师都读这个博客，津津乐道，每周两次（00:56:26听不清）干货满满。你也读过吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:56:29] Yeah. I used to be an engineer, and I was all up in that. And I think Coding Horror came from a... I forget the book, but there's a book with that graphic.
turns.zh: [00:56:29听不清]是啊，我以前也是工程师，对这个很着迷。我觉得《Coding Horror》源自一本……我忘了书名了，但有本图文并茂的书。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: There's a book, and there's a graphic. Yeah. And he wrote a post which really stuck with me for years. He said, how to be famous on the internet. He said, there's three simple steps. One, write a blog post. Two, do this three times a week. Three, do it for two years. And I guarantee, if you do this, you're going to be famous. And I always thought it's kind of ironic, but the more I read it, the more I thought he actually means something with it. And when I started this blog, The Pragmatic Engineer, I said, "I'm tired of my old blog being all over the place, and there's no focus, and no-one really cares about it. I'm going to do what Jeff Atwood said. I'm going to publish... Okay, it's not going to be twice a week, but every two weeks I'm going to publish an article, and I'll do it for a year." So I started to do this. I published six blog posts about software engineering, going into topics that I [inaudible 00:57:25] research and all that, and then I gave up.
turns.zh: 有一本书，还有一幅图。是的。他写了一篇帖子，多年来一直让我印象深刻。他说，如何在互联网上出名。他说，三个简单步骤。第一，写一篇博客文章。第二，每周做三次。第三，坚持两年。我保证，如果你这样做，你一定会出名的。我一直觉得这挺讽刺的，但读得越多，就越觉得他其实有深意。当我开始写《务实工程师》这个博客时，我说：“我厌倦了之前那个杂乱无章、没有重点、没人关心的老博客。我要按照杰夫·阿特伍德说的做。我每两周发布一篇文章，坚持一年。”于是我开始这样做了。我写了六篇关于软件工程的博文，内容都是我研究过的主题之类的，然后就放弃了。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And I'm saying this because I kind of gave up, and I left it for a few months, but then something interesting happened. I had a huge traffic spike, and it crashed my shared hosting at the time. And it came from a site called Hacker News that I [inaudible 00:57:41] heard about, and people were discussing my posts, and they were adding a lot of things. And I was like, that's interesting. People care about what I wrote six months ago.
turns.zh: 我之所以说这些，是因为我确实放弃了，放了几个月，但后来发生了件有趣的事。我的流量暴增，把当时用的共享主机都搞崩了。这源于一个叫Hacker News的网站，我[听不清00:57:25]听说过，人们在讨论我的帖子，添加了很多内容。我当时就想，真有意思。人们对六个月前我写的东西感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was that post, by the way?
turns.zh: 顺便说一下，那篇帖子叫什么？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: It was called, "A comment is an invitation for refactoring." I wrote my view that if there's a comment in a code, that means that comment should be deleted and you should just refactor the whole thing. And it exploded on Hacker News. Some people called me an idiot, some people called me absolute wisdom, and it was these two crowds battling it out. And I was like, wow, I actually made software engineers in Silicon Valley argue about my stuff. I saw some of the [inaudible 00:58:17] people, some really high [inaudible 00:58:18] people were really going for [inaudible 00:58:21]. So that's when I thought [inaudible 00:58:23] my writings, some people might read it, it's not guaranteed.
turns.zh: 叫《评论是重构的邀请》。我写了自己的观点，认为如果代码中有评论，就应该删掉整个代码并重构。结果在Hacker News上炸了。有人说我是个白痴，也有人说我说得太对了，两派互相对线。当时我就想，哇，我居然让硅谷的软件工程师为我的观点争论不休。我看到一些[听不清00:58:17]人，还有一些非常资深的人[听不清00:58:18]都在激烈讨论。所以那时我才觉得[听不清00:58:23]我的文章可能会有人读，但不一定。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And I started to write on that blog once every few months, depending on my mood, but I never stopped doing it. And I partially did it [inaudible 00:58:35] always hoped that it would get onto this site called Hacker News. But by the way, for a while, I didn't even know you could submit it, so I never submitted my own things. But the other thing was, I just kind of liked it, and I had this habit, and over years... I had this blog from 2015. For six years I was writing that blog, and in the last year... When I worked at Uber, on the side I wrote about my work, in terms of the things that I could write about, not about the details that we did, but some of the learnings [inaudible 00:59:02] for example, distributed systems. And more and more of these posts just started to just pop up on Hacker News. People would either submit it, or sometimes when I submitted it, it would just do well. And I was thinking, so people... I started to get this validation, people care about what I write.
turns.zh: 后来我开始每隔几个月在那个博客上写一篇，视心情而定，但从未停止。部分原因是为了[听不清00:58:35]总希望能被Hacker News收录。不过有一阵子我甚至不知道能提交文章，所以从未提交过自己的内容。另外，我就是喜欢写作，养成了这个习惯，几年来……我从2015年就开了这个博客。坚持了六年，最近一年……在Uber工作时，我利用业余时间写写工作，比如可以写的部分，不是具体细节，而是一些经验，比如分布式系统。越来越多这类文章开始在Hacker News上火起来。人们要么主动提交，要么我自己提交后效果也不错。我就在想，原来人们……我开始获得认可，人们对我的写作感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And to question of the success of the newsletter, by the time I launched a newsletter, I had a lot of posts that a lot of software engineers read, and there was a very famous post about performance management, how to do performance reviews. I wrote one about the tri-modal nature of software engineering salaries, where I observed that there's three different tiers that are... There's big tech and there's local companies. And I think what happened is, when I announced that I'm going to write this newsletter, I also put it on the blog. A lot of people realize that they... "I've been reading this Pragmatic Engineer, I don't know who is behind it, but I like it. Let me sign up. I do want to get an email every week, instead of the things that were every now and then."
turns.zh: 至于通讯成功与否的问题。当时我推出通讯时，已经有许多软件工程师阅读我的文章，其中有一篇关于绩效管理、如何进行绩效评估的文章非常受欢迎。我还写过一篇关于软件工程师薪资三种模式的文章，指出存在三层薪资梯队——大型科技公司和本地公司。关键在于，当我宣布要写通讯时，同时把它发布到了博客上。许多读者意识到：“我一直读《务实工程师》，不知道幕后是谁，但很喜欢。让我订阅吧。我希望每周都能收到邮件，而不是偶尔才有消息。”

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So there was years of work, and I wish I could tell you how to build a successful newsletter, but the best advice I have is still what Jeff Atwood does, except I have less conviction. But if you start writing, and you do it regularly, two things will happen. First of all, you're going to [inaudible 01:00:11] you write for yourself and you keep improving, you'll be a better writer. That's for sure. If you're lucky or if you're right about stuff, you might start to attract people who think similarly. So step one is get started. Step two is keep it up. And my suggestion is [inaudible 01:00:26] for yourself. The weird thing is, until I started my newsletter, I never thought I would turn this ever into a business, but it always felt rewarding. So I never... If you're starting out writing a newsletter to do what I'm doing one day, it might work out. But interesting enough, I never even thought that this was an opportunity.
turns.zh: 这背后是多年的努力。我希望能告诉你如何打造成功的通讯，但我能给出的最佳建议还是借鉴Jeff Atwood的做法，虽然我没那么坚定。但只要开始写作并坚持下去，两件事就会发生。首先，你会不断提升自我——写作是为自己而写，水平会逐渐提高。这是肯定的。如果运气好，或者你的观点有价值，或许还能吸引志同道合的人。所以第一步是开始行动，第二步是坚持下去。我建议先为自己写作。奇怪的是，在推出通讯前，我从未想过要将其商业化，但这个过程始终充满回报。所以如果你刚开始写通讯，目标是像我一样发展，或许能成功。但有趣的是，我甚至从未把这视为一个机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So people listening to this that are thinking about, should I explore this life? If you think about your story, you wrote a book, you blogged for a while before this, you worked at Uber for a number of years. In a sense, it comes across a little bit like, there's no way I can be successful if that's the background I need to have. I have to have written things and worked at an awesome tech company. What advice do you give folks that are coming to you being like, "Gergely, should I start a newsletter? Does it make sense for me?" Do you need the background that you have, do you think?
turns.zh: 所以听众中那些想探索另一种生活的人，如果回顾你的经历——你写了本书，在此之前写博客，在Uber工作多年。从某种角度看，这似乎暗示：没有这样的背景就注定无法成功。我必须写过东西，还在顶尖科技公司工作过。那么对于那些问“格尔吉，我该不该开通通讯？这对我有意义吗？”的人，你会给出什么建议？你认为他们需要你所拥有的背景吗？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Don't forget that when I started my blog, I didn't have any of this.
turns.zh: 别忘了，我刚开始写博客时可没有这些背景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is while you were at Uber. This is before you started the newsletter.
turns.zh: 那是在你Uber任职期间。通讯推出前。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: It was before I was at Uber. So I was maybe at Skyscanner, or maybe at Skype, but I was even blogging before. I was talking to conferences before. So my advice really would be, if you're thinking of a newsletter or something similar, start teaching and sharing what you know and what you're observing. This could be a newsletter, this could be a YouTube video, this could be going to meetup. Actually, ten years ago I went to a lot of meetups where I presented all sorts [inaudible 01:01:54] I met a lot of cool people. I would say, share your knowledge one way or the other. And as you're doing it, you're going to learn a lot more.
turns.zh: 那是在我加入Uber之前。所以那时我可能在Skyscanner工作，或者在Skype，但甚至在此之前我就开始写博客了。我还参加过各种会议。所以我的建议是，如果你在考虑通讯或类似项目，先开始教学，分享你的知识和观察。这可以是通讯，可以是YouTube视频，可以参加聚会。事实上，十年前我参加过很多聚会，分享各种观点[inaudible 01:01:54]，结识了很多很酷的人。我会说，无论用哪种方式，分享你的知识。在实践的过程中，你会学到更多。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So what I find... This is true, when I was a manager, we had to set goals, and I told people there's two types of goals you can set. One is [inaudible 01:02:12] people set this goal, I want to be promoted the next thing, or I want to lead this big project. And those are bad goals, because it's not in your control. So setting a goal that I want to have a successful newsletter with, I don't know, 20,000 subscribers, that's a goal where you're not in charge. A good goal is what you can do. So a good goal for example is, I want to learn this new language in the next year, which I'm going to spend time on, or I want to leave work at 5:00 PM on Fridays to be home with family. So set those goals that you can control.
turns.zh: 接下来我发现……这是真的。我当经理时，我们需要设定目标。我告诉员工，你们可以设定两种类型的目标。一种是[听不清 01:02:12]这种目标，比如“我想升职”或者“我想负责这个大项目”。但这种目标不靠谱，因为它们不受你控制。设定一个目标，比如“我想让通讯订阅量达到2万”，这就不是你能掌控的了。好的目标应该是你能做到的。比如“我要在一年内学会一门新语言”，这样你就能把时间投入其中；或者“每周五下午5点准时下班，回家陪家人”。这些才是你能掌控的目标。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And this is how actually my blog started initially. My goal was, I want to write once a month. And I did that for a while, and I was proud about that. Or whenever I learn something, I actually want to share it every now and then. So I would say set those goals, and the rest will come, probably. Again, don't get me wrong, I'm not trying to talk people out of doing it. But for me, a lot of this was luck. And the other thing that I would suggest is be curious, and look at your professional career as well. One thing that definitely helped me is getting pedigree. I come from a small country, from a really good university which no-one knows about, but I didn't grow up in let's say Silicon Valley, so I actually made a subconscious point to try to work my way up. And after I got to let's say JPMorgan in London, I was pretty picky of where I would go next. So that's why, when Skype came along [inaudible 01:03:36] this is great. Everyone knows Skype, I love Skype. And it was same thing with Uber.
turns.zh: 事实上，我的博客最初就是这样起步的。我的目标是每月写一篇文章。我坚持了一段时间，为此感到自豪。或者每当我学到新东西时，都会时不时分享出来。总之，设定这些你能掌控的目标，其他的自然会水到渠成。别误会，我不是想劝别人别这么做。但对我来说，很多成功都是靠运气的。另外，我建议大家保持好奇心，也要审视自己的职业生涯。对我来说，获得专业背景很有帮助。我来自一个小国家，毕业于一所鲜为人知的优秀大学，但我没有在硅谷长大，所以我下意识地努力往上爬。到了伦敦的摩根大通后，我对下一份工作的选择变得很挑剔。这就是为什么Skype出现时（[听不清 01:03:36]）我很兴奋。大家都知道Skype，我也喜欢Skype。优步的情况也一样。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So especially these days, people would not pay nearly as much attention to me if I worked at Small Parts Limited. So there's that part as well. So you need to manage some of these things, figure out what you want to do. For a long time, I pretty much thought that I just want to climb the corporate ladder and prove that I'm good enough at all these companies. I was just doing all this stuff on the side. It's interesting how it's now flipped, and now doing these things, this is my main thing, which used to be my side project.
turns.zh: 如今尤其如此，如果我在小零件有限公司工作，几乎没人会关注我。所以这也是个关键点。你需要管理好这些事情，明确自己的目标。很长一段时间，我以为只要在大公司爬升阶梯，证明自己足够优秀就行了。我只是在业余时间做这些事情。很有趣的是，现在情况反过来了，现在做这些事情成了我的主业，而曾经只是副业。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And I guess one last advice is, do some side projects. All of this starts as a side project. At work, no-one's really going to appreciate that you're doing a newsletter or this or that. Try stuff on the side, assuming that you have time. Or if you don't have time, try to make time. Because I feel a lot of what we're doing is pretty entrepreneurial, and the only way you're going to get these muscles, if you start some small things.
turns.zh: 最后一条建议是，尝试做些副业。所有事情都是从副业开始的。在工作中，没人会真正欣赏你做通讯或其他事情。先在业余时间尝试，假设你有时间的话。即使没时间，也要挤出时间。因为我觉得我们所做的大部分事情都带有创业精神，如果你想锻炼这些能力，就得从小事做起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talk about the pedigree being important. I think there's also an even deeper point, that you actually need real experience doing real things that scaled and worked and mattered and worked with amazing people, to actually build a foundation to write about, share wisdom from. And that's really important. There's a lot of people starting newsletters and tweeting who haven't done much and don't have a lot of real life experience to share. And I think that's the core of a lot of what we do, is it needs to be based on real things that worked and that you've learned, or that you have access to other people who have learned these things.
turns.zh: 你提到背景很重要。我认为还有更深层的一点，那就是你需要真正做过成功且有影响力的事情，与优秀的人合作过，这样才能积累写作和分享智慧的基础。这真的很重要。很多新手写通讯、发推特的人，都没做过什么事，也没有太多真实生活经验可分享。我认为这正是我们工作的核心所在——必须基于真实有效的经验，或者能接触到那些有经验的人。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I would say that, but one thing that I'll double down [inaudible 01:05:09] that's a really good observation is, if you're serious, like one day I will want to write a book or a newsletter, it's kind of the same thing, or teach people about stuff, look at the people that you look up to that you actually trust. Maybe it's me a bit or maybe it's you, but it's more likely people like Kent Beck, for example. He's the creator of TDD, and he's written a lot of books. He's one of my favorite people, I think he's coming up 50 or 60 [inaudible 01:05:36] if he listens to this, sorry if... I don't want [inaudible 01:05:38] seem old, but what I love about Kent Beck, is he's been in the middle of it. He has always worked in the industry, and that he wrote about it. But for example, I think he invented or he was a co-inventor of... Was it TDD or extreme program... Anyway, one of these methodologies.
turns.zh: 我想说，但有一点我要强调[01:05:09不清]，这确实是个很棒的观察。如果你认真对待这件事，比如说，我未来想写本书或开通新闻通讯，这两者本质上是一样的，或者是教别人一些东西。看看你尊敬且真正信任的人吧。也许是有点像我，也许是像你，但更有可能是像肯特·贝克这样的人。他是测试驱动开发（TDD）的创始人，写了很多书。他是我最喜欢的作者之一，我觉得他快50或60岁了[01:05:36不清]。如果他听到这段话，还请别介意……我不想显得自己老了，但我喜欢肯特·贝克的地方在于，他始终身处行业前沿。他一直在业界工作，并将这些经验写成书。但比如说，我认为他发明了或者是共同发明了……是TDD还是极限编程……总之是这些方法论之一。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And then [inaudible 01:05:58] went to work at Facebook. He took a title cut to be a software engineer, and then he hosts the TDD workshop, the test driven development workshop, and no-one showed up at Facebook. And Facebook did no testing, which went against all commercial wisdom. And he took that risk joining this company where he could have been... People would've knelt down to him anywhere else, but he went to this company where he just wanted to learn. He's this lifelong learner. He's right now writing a book. But what I think [inaudible 01:06:26] if you want to be someone who people listen to, yes, do cool and interesting stuff, push yourself to get into places that do these interesting things.
turns.zh: 然后[01:05:58不清]他去了Facebook。他降职成为一名软件工程师，然后主持测试驱动开发（TDD）研讨会，但Facebook根本没人参加。Facebook根本不做测试，这完全违背了商业常识。他冒险加入了这家公司，在那里他本可以成为……在其他任何地方，人们都会对他毕恭毕敬，但他选择了这家公司，只是想学习。他是个终身学习者。他现在正在写书。但我认为[01:06:26不清]如果你想成为人们愿意倾听的人，是的，要做酷炫有趣的事，挑战自己进入那些正在做这些有趣事的团队。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: That's how, when I went to Uber in 2016, it was one of the highest regarded places back in 2016, and in 2017 it was the other way around. But back in 2016, people were turning down Facebook and Google offers to go at Uber, which we all thought would change the world. So you do need to get into those teams that are doing interesting stuff, prove that you can do that, and you'll have a lot more interesting stories to share, that's for sure.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么我2016年加入Uber时，它在2016年还备受推崇，但2017年情况却反转了。但2016年时，人们拒绝Facebook和谷歌的offer，选择加入Uber，我们都认为Uber会改变世界。所以你确实需要加入那些正在做有趣事的团队，证明自己能胜任这项工作，这样你就能有更多有趣的故事可分享，这点毋庸置疑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you had to boil down advice for how to be successful in this life of a newsletter, you had to boil it down to just one or two key pieces of advice, what would you say?
turns.zh: 如果你要总结如何在新闻通讯领域成功的建议，必须归结为一两个关键点，你会说什么？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: One is habit of depth in the field, whatever field you do. So this might mean that I think... I don't want to say that if you don't have experience, don't start one, but it's kind of true. So become an expert somewhere, somehow, before you start, because you'll be a lot more credible. I think there's no shortage of reporters and journalists who don't know about stuff, but they can interview people, but that doesn't give anything extra, and I think people feel that.
turns.zh: 第一点是，在你所从事的任何领域，都要养成深度钻研的习惯。这可能意味着……我不想说如果你没有经验就别开始，但这确实有道理。所以在开始之前，先成为某个领域的专家，这样你会更具可信度。我觉得不缺乏那些对某些领域一无所知却能采访他人的记者和新闻工作者，但这并不能带来任何附加价值，我觉得人们能感觉到这一点。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So I would say choose a field that you're going to be good at. And you can start on the side, doing this. Assuming you have something, you're someone with experience in the industry or you have insights, wisdom, observations to share, start doing so, in whatever format. I do newsletters. There's actually YouTube, a lot of people are becoming pretty successful on YouTube sharing their thing. Three, have a cadence and stick to it, to some extent, because you do need to keep repeating it. And then four, don't be afraid to try out new things. A good example of a person who did these is Steve Yegge. Steve Yegge is... Have you heard of Steve Yegge?
turns.zh: 因此，我会建议你选择一个你擅长的领域。可以先兼职做这件事。假设你有相关经验、行业洞察或独特见解，不妨以任何形式开始分享。我自己就做新闻通讯。YouTube平台上也有很多人通过分享内容取得了不错的成绩。第三，要保持一定的更新频率，因为内容需要反复输出，才能形成影响力。第四，不要害怕尝试新事物。史蒂夫·耶格（Steve Yegge）就是一个很好的例子。你听说过他吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. He wrote some epic long...
turns.zh: 是的。他写过一些长篇巨著……

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: He used to work at Amazon, and then at Google he wrote this internal email about platforms, about how Amazon is great at platforms and Google is terrible. And he was really well known at Google, because he wrote stuff inside Google. So he's experienced, knows a lot of stuff, and then he quit Google and he started to do a podcast that's on YouTube. You could check it out, it's called Stevey's Podcast. And what he did is, every week he recorded an episode and he talked about a bunch of his learnings, a lot of stuff, and he was pretty clear up front when he started the first one, he said, "What I'm doing is, I'm going to do this for six months and I'll see if it sticks, see if people care about it or people watch it."
turns.zh: 他曾在亚马逊工作，后来在谷歌时，他写了一封关于平台的内部邮件，指出亚马逊在平台方面做得很出色，而谷歌则做得很糟糕。他在谷歌非常有名，因为他在谷歌内部写了很多东西。所以他经验丰富，见多识广，后来离开谷歌，开始做YouTube播客。你可以去看看，叫《Stevey's Podcast》。他每周录制一期节目，分享自己的学习心得，内容丰富有趣。他在第一期节目开头就明确表示：“我会坚持做六个月，看看是否能持续下去，看看人们是否感兴趣、是否会观看。”

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Now, this guy had a lot of experience, really fun [inaudible 01:08:59] I think it's really fun to listen to. And in the end, it was I think successful. It got a couple thousand or maybe even 10,000 subscribers, but it wasn't this rocket ship. And I think what he did, he just stopped after six months, and he actually started head of engineering at Sourcegraph, he actually went back [inaudible 01:09:15] industry. But what I love about this, it shows that you cannot guarantee having success, but you can do what he did, which is start something, do a cadence, see if it sticks. If not, either pivot or do something else. I feel the world is kind of about that as well.
turns.zh: 这个人经验丰富，内容很有趣，听起来很棒。最终，播客确实成功了，有几千甚至一万订阅者，但算不上火爆。他六个月后停止更新，转而加入Sourcegraph担任工程总监，重返行业。但我觉得这件事说明，你无法保证成功，但你可以像他一样先行动起来，保持节奏，看看是否能持续。如果不行，要么调整方向，要么尝试新事物。我觉得这个世界本质上也是如此。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: If you think about... Take a step back of, what is a successful newsletter? What is a successful podcast? What is a successful YouTube channel? And it's stuff that's interesting. It's either entertaining or educational. But all of these things, you can't really put a finger on. If you watch YouTube, Mr. Beast is someone who you probably came across, I actually like watching his videos and [inaudible 01:09:56] how good he does it, but it's not something you can [inaudible 01:09:59] anyone would have written in a book. So there is a sense of trying to understand what people care about, and a good way to understand is either experiment or observe or just try out stuff.
turns.zh: 如果你回想一下……退一步说，什么样的新闻通讯算成功？什么样的播客算成功？什么样的YouTube频道算成功？这些都需要有趣，要么娱乐性强，要么有教育意义。但所有这些东西，你都无法用一句话概括。如果你看YouTube，可能听说过“Mr. Beast”，他的内容很有趣，我也喜欢看他的视频，但这不是任何人能写进书里的。所以关键在于了解人们关心什么，而了解的方法就是尝试、观察或实践。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is great. I feel like I can boil this down even further from everything you just said, which is, build depth in an area, then write a blog post twice a week for two years, and good things will happen.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得我可以把你刚才说的总结得更简洁：在一个领域深耕，然后两年内每周写两篇博客，好的事情自然会发生。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I'm pretty sure. And here's an interesting thought as well, just for closure. I was talking with someone on why my newsletter is so successful. It's really successful, and I honestly don't know why. And this person told me something interesting. This is a person who had a really successful YouTube channel with about 200,000 subscribers, so more than my newsletter. And he said this. He's like, "What I noticed is, you started your blog in 2015, 2016, and I started my YouTube channel in 2019 or something like that. And on YouTube, there's so much quality, there's super high great productions, everyone is doing YouTube." And he said, "You know what I don't see? I don't see many blogs that are writing in depth stuff regularly. I feel everyone went over to YouTube or TikTok. So there is the other angle of the medium." And I'm saying this, not [inaudible 01:11:16] but it might be an advantage. These days, fewer people write, because I think a lot of people find it hard and more people will do videos. And you can take advantage of some of these shifts, which might be good or bad.
turns.zh:
我很确定。最后再分享一个有趣的想法。跟某人聊起为什么我的新闻通讯如此成功。确实很成功，但说实话我也不知道原因。这位朋友提到一个有趣的观点。他曾经营一个YouTube频道，订阅量超过20万，比我的新闻通讯订阅量还多。他说：“我注意到你2015年、2016年开始写博客，而我2019年左右才开通YouTube频道。YouTube上有很多高质量的内容，制作精良，每个人都在做YouTube。但我很少看到有博客定期输出深度内容。大家似乎都转向了YouTube或TikTok。”这让我看到了另一种媒体生态视角。

我不是说[01:11:16的模糊语音]，但这或许是一种优势。如今写作的人越来越少，因为很多人觉得写作太难了，而制作视频的人则越来越多。你可以利用这些转变带来的机遇，无论是利好还是弊端。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So if you're going to be a really well known person on YouTube, you might get more people watching you, but you'll have a lot more competition. And the last thing is that for me, writing, especially with software engineers, it's really efficient, because I can scan through it. I don't like YouTube videos, especially for learning about stuff, because I can't even scan through the whole thing. It's just really time consuming.
turns.zh: 所以如果你想在YouTube上成为知名人物，可能会吸引更多观众，但竞争也会更激烈。对我来说，写作（尤其是面向软件工程师的写作）效率更高，因为我可以快速浏览内容。我不喜欢YouTube视频，尤其是用于学习的视频，因为根本没法快速浏览整个内容，太浪费时间了。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: So I think, decide if you want to do entertainment, which for these podcast listeners, I don't think that's in the question, you're competing with the likes of Spotify and Netflix. Education, which is a little bit more dry, but it's really useful. Or edutainment, which is entertaining education. And once you figure that out, either if it's education or edutainment, you can figure out what format might work both for the medium and for you. And at end of the day, you need to enjoy it. I personally have learned over time to love writing. I love being in the zone. So for me it's not really work, but it's fun. And once you find that thing, whatever that might be, it just makes it easier.
turns.zh: 所以要决定是做娱乐内容（对播客听众来说，这显然不是问题，因为你要和Spotify、Netflix等平台竞争），还是做更枯燥但实用性的教育内容，或者是寓教于乐的教育内容。一旦确定方向，无论是教育还是寓教于乐，都能找到适合平台和自身的形式。最重要的是，要享受这个过程。我个人随着时间的推移逐渐爱上了写作，喜欢进入心流状态。对我来说，这不算工作，而是乐趣。当你找到热爱的事情时，成功就水到渠成了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Gergely, it's always so fun talking about newsletter stuff. I don't have many people to talk about this life with. I hope this was useful to people who are exploring this path, thinking about it, or even the different creator path. Just two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out or learn more? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 格尔格利，聊新闻通讯相关的话题总是很有趣。我没有太多人可以一起探讨这些话题。希望这对正在探索这条路径、思考相关问题的人，或者甚至是不同创作者路径的人有所帮助。最后两个问题：如果想联系你或了解更多信息，哪里可以找到你？听众如何能对你有所帮助？

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: You can find me at pragmaticengineer.com. There is a bunch of stuff listed there from the Twitter, LinkedIn, my talent collective, some of the companies that I invest in, et cetera. Everything's there. And you can also sign up to my newsletter. Listeners being useful to me... If you work in tech, consider signing up to my newsletter. I always tell people we're a complimentary newsletter. If you work in product or have an interest in product [inaudible 01:13:11] newsletter is an awesome choice. With software engineering management, it goes the other way. And it's not just... People are telling me when they're data scientists or even product folks, sometimes they get some value out of it.
turns.zh: 你可以在pragmaticengineer.com找到我。那里列出了我的Twitter、LinkedIn、人才库、投资的公司等所有信息。一切尽在那里。也可以订阅我的新闻通讯。听众如何能对我有帮助……如果你在科技行业工作，考虑订阅我的新闻通讯。我总是告诉人们，我们的通讯是互补的。如果你从事产品工作，或者对产品感兴趣[01:13:11的模糊语音]，订阅我的通讯是个绝佳选择。至于软件工程管理领域，情况则相反。这不只是……人们告诉我，数据科学家甚至产品人员有时也能从中获得价值。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: I write this column called the scoop every Thursday. If you hear of any interesting scoop happening, especially relevant for techies, this might be some change in the workplace, like your company is just rolling out agile [inaudible 01:13:36] team at Twitter did, feel free to ping me, just a short search for sending scoop to the Pragmatic Engineer. I treat everything as anonymous, so you can tell me interesting stuff. I'm typically interested in the stuff that you might not read about in the traditional media, but us techies really care about.
turns.zh: 每周四我都会写一篇名为《独家新闻》的专栏。如果你听说了任何有趣的独家消息，特别是与科技从业者相关的——比如你的公司正在推行敏捷开发（Twitter 团队最近就这么做了，但具体细节我这里就不透露了）——欢迎随时联系我，只需在搜索引擎中输入“向务实工程师投稿”即可。我会对所有信息保密，所以你可以放心分享那些传统媒体不会报道但我们科技从业者真正关心的内容。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: And finally, if you work at Google and you want anonymity to talk to me, just ping me, because one of my next articles will be Google's engineering culture. I wrote one about Facebook, one about Amazon, and I tried to talk with mostly software engineers to get a sense of how these companies work from a software engineer and engineer manager perspective.
turns.zh: 最后，如果你在谷歌工作并希望匿名与我交流，请随时联系我，因为我下一篇文章将聚焦谷歌的工程文化。此前我已写过关于 Facebook 和亚马逊的文章，采访了大量软件工程师和工程经理，旨在从他们的视角解析这些公司的运作模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I hope this comes out before that post comes out, but if not, then enjoy that post. Gergely, thank you so much for being here. This was awesome. And maybe we'll do a V2 as things continue to grow.
turns.zh: 太棒了。希望这段翻译能在那篇文章发布前完成，如果没能做到，那就好好享受那篇内容吧。格尔盖利，非常感谢你能来参加节目。这次交流太棒了。随着节目影响力不断扩大，也许我们会推出第二版。

turns.speaker: Gergely Orosz
turns.en: Awesome. It was great being here, Lenny.
turns.zh: 太棒了。伦尼，很高兴能来参加节目。
